alt: Three agar cubes of side 1 cm, 2 cm and 3 cm: surface area 6, 24 and 54 square centimetres, volume 1, 8 and 27 cubic centimetres, so the surface area to volume ratio falls from 6 to 1, to 3 to 1, to 2 to 1 and the largest cube takes longest to turn colourless.
caption: Figure: the bigger the cube, the smaller its surface area to volume ratio

alt: Pedigree of the Ncube family: Mr and Mrs Ncube (both Aa, no albinism) have three children, Thandeka and Nomsa without albinism and Sipho, shown shaded, who has albinism and is aa; two unaffected parents with an affected child shows the allele for albinism is recessive.
caption: Figure: pedigree diagram of albinism in the Ncube family

alt: An alveolus beside a capillary: oxygen diffuses from the air in the alveolus into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses the other way, across two walls that are each one cell thick, so the diffusion distance is very short and a dense blood supply keeps the concentration gradients steep.
caption: Figure: gas exchange between an alveolus and a capillary by diffusion

alt: Bacterial cell: a cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm with ribosomes, a single loop of circular DNA lying free in the cytoplasm and small rings called plasmids; there is no nucleus and no mitochondria.
caption: Figure: a bacterial cell has circular DNA and plasmids but no nucleus

alt: Histogram of 20 bean pod lengths in 2 cm classes: frequencies 2, 4, 7, 5 and 2 with touching bars, peaking in the 13.0 to 14.9 cm modal class and falling on both sides, which shows continuous variation.
caption: Figure: a histogram of bean pod lengths shows continuous variation

alt: Negative feedback controlling blood glucose: if glucose rises above the set point the pancreas secretes more insulin, the liver turns glucose into glycogen and cells take up glucose so the level falls back; if it falls below the set point the pancreas secretes glucagon and the liver breaks glycogen down to glucose so the level rises back to the set point.
caption: Figure: negative feedback keeps the blood glucose concentration near its set point

alt: Cross-sections of the three blood vessels: an artery with a thick muscular and elastic wall and a narrow lumen for high-pressure blood, a vein with a thin wall, a wide lumen and valves, and a capillary whose wall is one cell thick with a lumen only wide enough for one red blood cell.
caption: Figure: cross-sections of an artery, a vein and a capillary

alt: Front view of the breathing system: air passes down the trachea, which is held open by rings of cartilage, into a bronchus for each lung, then along branching bronchioles to the alveoli; the ribs with the intercostal muscles surround the lungs and the dome-shaped diaphragm lies beneath them.
caption: Figure: the human breathing system in front view

alt: Carbon cycle: plants take carbon dioxide from the air by photosynthesis, animals get carbon by feeding, respiration by plants, animals and decomposers returns carbon dioxide to the air, dead remains are broken down by decomposers or fossilised into fossil fuels, and combustion of fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide.
caption: Figure: the carbon cycle, showing photosynthesis, feeding, respiration, decomposition, fossilisation and combustion

alt: Front view of the digestive system: the mouth and salivary glands, oesophagus, stomach on the reader's right, liver on the reader's left with the gall bladder beneath it, pancreas below the stomach, coiled small intestine framed by the colon, then the rectum and anus.
caption: Figure: the human digestive system in front view, labelled

alt: DNA as a twisted ladder: two sugar-phosphate backbone strands coiled into a double helix, joined by rungs of bases held by weak hydrogen bonds, with A always pairing with T and C always pairing with G, so the two strands are complementary.
caption: Figure: the structure of DNA, a double helix with base pairs A-T and C-G

alt: Double circulation: the right side of the heart pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs in the pulmonary artery and oxygenated blood returns to the left side in the pulmonary veins; the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body in the aorta and deoxygenated blood returns to the right side in the vena cava, so blood passes through the heart twice per circuit.
caption: Figure: double circulation, the pulmonary circuit through the lungs and the systemic circuit through the body

alt: Antagonistic muscles at the elbow: to bend the arm the biceps on the front of the upper arm contracts and the triceps on the back relaxes, pulling the radius so the forearm rises; to straighten the arm the triceps contracts and the biceps relaxes.
caption: Figure: the biceps and triceps work as an antagonistic pair at the elbow

alt: Pyramid of energy for the grassland example, drawn to scale: grass 24 000 kJ per square metre per year, impala 1800 and lion 216; only 7.5% of the energy passes from grass to impala and 12% from impala to lion, so each bar is narrower than the one below.
caption: Figure: a pyramid of energy with bars drawn to scale (kJ per square metre per year)

alt: Graph of enzyme rate against pH for three enzymes: pepsin peaks at about pH 2 in the stomach, salivary amylase at about pH 7 in the mouth and trypsin at about pH 8 in the small intestine; each rate falls on both sides of its optimum pH.
caption: Figure: each enzyme has its own optimum pH, and the rate falls on both sides of it

alt: Graph of enzyme rate against temperature: the rate is low but not zero at 0 to 10 degrees Celsius, rises to a peak at the optimum of about 37 degrees Celsius, then falls much more steeply to zero by about 60 degrees Celsius as the enzyme is denatured.
caption: Figure: the effect of temperature on the rate of an enzyme reaction

alt: Horizontal section of the eye: light enters through the cornea, aqueous humour, pupil in the iris and the lens (held by suspensory ligaments and ciliary muscle), crosses the vitreous humour and is focused on the retina at the fovea; the optic nerve leaves at the blind spot.
caption: Figure: the structure of the human eye in horizontal section

alt: An insect-pollinated flower cut lengthways: sepals and large petals surround the stamens, each with an anther on a filament, and the carpel, which has a sticky stigma, a style and an ovary containing ovules; a nectary at the base of the petals makes nectar, and the flower sits on the receptacle at the top of the pedicel.
caption: Figure: an insect-pollinated flower cut lengthways, with its parts labelled

alt: Graph of Tatenda's pulse after two minutes of skipping: 126 beats per minute straight after exercise, then 108, 90, 78 and 72 over four minutes, back to the resting rate of 72, so the increase was 54 beats per minute (75%) and the recovery time 4 minutes.
caption: Figure: pulse rate after exercise falls back to the resting rate of 72 beats per minute in 4 minutes

alt: Front view of the heart: deoxygenated blood enters the right atrium from the vena cava and leaves the right ventricle by the pulmonary artery; oxygenated blood enters the left atrium from the pulmonary veins and leaves the left ventricle, which has the thickest wall, by the aorta; a septum separates the two sides.
caption: Figure: the structure of the heart seen from the front, with the vessels and valves labelled

alt: Food web from the Hwange table: grass and the leaves of trees and shrubs are the producers; termites, zebra, impala, kudu, giraffe and elephant are primary consumers; the aardvark, lion, leopard and wild dog are secondary consumers, and the impala is eaten by lion, leopard and wild dog, so it sits in several food chains.
caption: Figure: part of a food web in Hwange, with arrows pointing from food to feeder

alt: Transverse section of a leaf from top to bottom: waxy cuticle, upper epidermis, tightly packed palisade mesophyll full of chloroplasts, spongy mesophyll with air spaces, a vascular bundle with xylem above and phloem below, and a lower epidermis with a stoma between two guard cells through which carbon dioxide enters.
caption: Figure: a transverse section of a leaf with its layers labelled

alt: Graph from Example 2: at 0.04% carbon dioxide the rate rises from 10 to 30 and levels off from light intensity 4; at 0.10% carbon dioxide it is the same up to intensity 2, then climbs higher to about 46, showing light limits the rate first and then carbon dioxide.
caption: Figure: rate of photosynthesis against light intensity at two carbon dioxide concentrations

alt: Life cycle of the malaria parasite Plasmodium: an infected female Anopheles mosquito injects parasites that multiply in the liver, then in red blood cells which burst causing fever; sexual forms stay in the blood, another mosquito sucks them up, they reproduce in the mosquito and move to its salivary glands, ready to infect the next person.
caption: Figure: the life cycle of the malaria parasite in a person and in the Anopheles mosquito

alt: Hormone levels over a 28-day menstrual cycle: FSH is high in the first days, oestrogen rises to a peak around day 12, LH surges sharply around day 13 to 14 and ovulation follows, then progesterone rises to a peak around day 21 and falls towards day 28; the uterus lining is lost in days 1 to 5, repaired and thickened in days 6 to 13 and maintained in days 15 to 28.
caption: Figure: hormone levels and the uterus lining across a 28-day menstrual cycle

alt: Mitosis versus meiosis using a cell with 4 chromosomes: in mitosis the chromosomes are copied and the cell divides once into two genetically identical cells with 4 chromosomes each (human 46 to 46 and 46); in meiosis the cell divides twice into four genetically different cells with half the chromosomes, 2 each (human 46 to 23).
caption: Figure: mitosis makes two identical cells, meiosis makes four different cells with half the chromosomes (4 chromosomes shown for clarity)

alt: A nephron: filtration at the glomerulus forces water, glucose, urea and ions out of the blood into the capsule while blood cells and protein stay in the blood; reabsorption along the tubule returns all the glucose, most of the water and some ions to the blood capillaries; urea, excess water and ions continue down the collecting duct to the pelvis as urine.
caption: Figure: a nephron showing filtration, reabsorption and the formation of urine

alt: Nitrogen cycle: nitrogen-fixing bacteria and lightning turn nitrogen gas into usable compounds, decomposers turn the proteins and urea of dead organisms into ammonium ions, nitrifying bacteria turn ammonium into nitrate, plants absorb nitrate to make protein, animals eat the plants, and denitrifying bacteria return nitrate to nitrogen gas.
caption: Figure: the nitrogen cycle with the four groups of bacteria and decomposers

alt: Plant cell and animal cell side by side: both have a cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria and ribosomes; only the plant cell also has a cellulose cell wall, a large permanent vacuole full of cell sap and chloroplasts.
caption: Figure: a plant cell and an animal cell with their main structures labelled

alt: Plant cells in three solutions: in pure water or a dilute solution water enters and the cell is turgid; in a solution as concentrated as the cell sap there is no net movement and the cell is flaccid; in a concentrated solution water leaves and the membrane pulls away from the wall, called plasmolysis.
caption: Figure: a plant cell is turgid in water, flaccid in an equal solution and plasmolysed in a concentrated solution

alt: Pondweed apparatus: a lamp at a measured distance from a boiling tube of water and sodium hydrogencarbonate holding pondweed with its cut end up, inside a beaker of water; oxygen bubbles from the cut end are counted per minute at each lamp distance.
caption: Figure: apparatus for investigating how light intensity affects the rate of photosynthesis

alt: Genetic diagram for two heterozygous round-seeded pea plants, Rr crossed with Rr: each parent makes R and r gametes, the Punnett square gives RR, Rr, Rr and rr, so the offspring genotypes are 1 RR to 2 Rr to 1 rr and the phenotypes are 3 round to 1 wrinkled.
caption: Figure: genetic diagram and Punnett square for Rr x Rr

alt: Reflex arc for stepping on a thorn: pain receptors in the skin send impulses along a sensory neurone to a relay neurone in the spinal cord, which passes them to a motor neurone that carries them to a leg muscle, the effector, which contracts to lift the foot; other impulses reach the brain a moment later.
caption: Figure: a reflex arc from receptor to effector, with a separate pathway to the brain

alt: Section through the skin from the surface inwards: epidermis, dermis containing a hair in its follicle with a hair erector muscle, a coiled sweat gland with a duct to a pore, temperature receptors with sensory neurones, and blood vessels with capillaries near the surface, and a layer of fatty tissue beneath.
caption: Figure: a section through the skin with the parts that control body temperature

alt: Six specialised cells with the feature that suits each job: ciliated cell with cilia that sweep mucus, root hair cell with a long thin extension, red blood cell that is a biconcave disc with no nucleus, sperm cell with a tail and mitochondria, palisade cell packed with chloroplasts and neurone with a long fibre.
caption: Figure: six specialised cells, each with a structure that suits its function

alt: Graph of the lesson's sweet potato results: mean change in mass falls from +15.0% in pure water to −16.0% in 1.0 mol per dm³ sucrose, crossing 0% at about 0.45 mol per dm³, where there is no net movement of water.
caption: Figure: percentage change in mass of sweet potato against sucrose concentration

alt: Bar chart of tongue rolling in a class of 40 students: 26 (65%) can roll their tongue and 14 (35%) cannot, drawn as two separate bars with a gap because the feature falls into distinct categories with no intermediates, which is discontinuous variation.
caption: Figure: a bar chart with a gap between the bars shows discontinuous variation

alt: The urinary system: two kidneys, each receiving blood with urea through a renal artery and returning filtered blood by a renal vein, a ureter from each kidney carrying urine to the bladder, and the urethra carrying urine from the bladder out of the body.
caption: Figure: the urinary system with the blood vessels of the kidneys

alt: Yeast growth curve from Example 2: numbers rise slowly from 2 to 3 thousand per cubic millimetre in the lag phase to 2 hours, then steeply through 8, 24 and 52 thousand in the exponential phase, and level off near 74 thousand in the stationary phase after about 10 hours.
caption: Figure: the sigmoid growth curve of yeast in sugar solution
